analysis.one_liner: Triples back pay for workers illegally fired for union activity and lets them sue for punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with no cosponsors, it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, when an employer illegally fires a worker for union activity, the National Labor Relations Board can only order reinstatement and ordinary back pay — a penalty many employers treat as a manageable cost of breaking the law. This bill would have required the Board to award triple back pay in such cases and would have let the fired worker go to federal court to seek additional compensatory and punitive damages, or to state court for a wrongful-discharge claim. It was referred to a House committee and a subcommittee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are fired or penalized for exercising rights under the National Labor Relations Act. They would recover three times their wage rate in back pay from the Board, plus the option to sue in federal court for compensatory and punitive damages against the employer that fired them illegally. Unions and workers organizing new shops would also gain, since harsher penalties deter employers from firing union supporters.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the National Labor Relations Board to award back pay equal to three times the employee's wage rate when the Board finds an employee was discharged in violation of the National Labor Relations Act, and to notify the employee of the right to sue. [S2] [S3]

Makes it unlawful for an employer to discharge an employee for exercising rights protected under the National Labor Relations Act, and allows the worker to file a civil action in federal district court, regardless of the amount in controversy, to recover punitive damages, or in state court to recover wrongful-discharge damages. [S3]

Under existing law the Board's remedies in illegal-firing cases are limited to reinstatement and ordinary back pay, so the bill would have made illegal anti-union firings materially more expensive for employers. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Employers found to have illegally discharged employees for union activity. They would owe triple back pay and potentially large court judgments, and would face greater litigation exposure and settlement pressure in unfair labor practice cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers that illegally fire union supporters

drawbacks.text: Employers and business groups have long argued that NLRA remedies should stay modest and discretionary; tripling back pay and adding punitive damages could impose outsized penalties for a single violation and drive more unfair labor practice disputes into court litigation, raising costs and delays for both sides. [S2] [S3]

The bill applies only to discharge cases, leaving other unfair labor practices (such as threats, surveillance, or refusal to bargain) under the old, weaker remedies, so its deterrent effect would be uneven. [S2] [S3]
Opening state-court wrongful-discharge suits on top of federal remedies could produce duplicative litigation and inconsistent outcomes across states. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is real: today an employer can illegally fire a union activist, drag out proceedings for years, and owe only the ordinary back pay it would have owed anyway, which makes firing union supporters a rational business bet. The bill would have changed that arithmetic. The honest cost is that penalties would fall only on employers who lose at the Board, but those penalties would be substantially larger, and the added litigation could cut both ways for workers. The bill was a single-page remedy bill with no cosponsors, so it was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee and then to its Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee in July 1996, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey, a New York Democrat, introduced the bill on July 9, 1996. [S1] [S5]
No member signed on as a cosponsor. [S4]

The House referred it to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities on the day of introduction, and on July 19, 1996 to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations; those were the last actions of the bill. [S5]
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill died without any hearing or vote; most bills that stall in subcommittee never reach the floor. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers keep the current low cost of illegally firing union supporters: ordinary back pay only, no punitive damages, no treble award. Workers fired for union activity get no new remedies.

for.name: Rep. Maurice D. Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Labor Relations Remedies Act to add treble back pay and court remedies for workers fired in violation of the National Labor Relations Act.

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities (104th Congress, Republican majority)
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 9, 1996 and referred it to the Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled. [S5]

against.name: Employer and business community
against.role: Opponents of expanded National Labor Relations Act penalties
against.what_they_did: Business groups have historically opposed treble damages and punitive remedies in labor law on the ground that they would raise the cost of employment disputes; no organized support for the bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no roll-call breakdown exists; the sponsor was a Democrat and the House majority and committee of referral were Republican. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: If enacted, employers would pay triple back pay and face punitive-damage suits when they illegally fire workers, raising the cost of anti-union retaliation. Their current interest in keeping those penalties small runs against workers who want a real deterrent.
Harsher penalties for illegally firing union supporters would make organizing drives and bargaining safer for workers, which is where unions recruit and represent members.
